candidates.label: A
candidates.abstract: Datacenter inference hardware must deliver throughput within application response-time limits. We evaluate a deployed Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) on six production MLP, CNN, and LSTM models representing 95% of the provider's inference demand at the time, comparing contemporary Intel Haswell and Nvidia K80 platforms. The host-controlled coprocessor combines a 65,536-unit, 8-bit integer systolic Matrix Multiply Unit with a software-managed Unified Buffer and deterministic execution. Its 92-trillion-operations-per-second peak does not by itself describe service throughput: measurements enforce latency limits and include host interaction overhead. TPU throughput relative to Haswell is 14.5× by geometric mean and 29.2× by production-weighted mean; corresponding ratios against K80 are 13.2× and 15.3×. Complete-server performance per watt is 17–34× Haswell and 14–16× K80, depending on averaging. These comparisons use quantized TPU inference against floating-point CPU and GPU execution. Roofline and counter analysis identify memory limits in MLP/LSTM workloads, explaining why low utilization can coexist with high relative throughput. Energy proportionality is also limited: CNN0 at 10% offered load consumes 88% of full-load TPU power. Modeled alternatives explore hardware changes, including higher memory bandwidth, separately from deployed measurements. The results characterize inference specialization under production constraints; energy efficiency is a disclosed proxy, while purchase prices and total ownership cost remain undisclosed.
introduction: The usefulness of a datacenter inference accelerator depends on the service it can sustain under a response-time limit. Increasing batch size can raise arithmetic throughput while making individual requests wait too long. Tail latency is therefore part of the evaluation target, consistent with the concern articulated in The Tail at Scale [dean2013tail]. For MLP0 in this study, the limit is 7 ms at the 99th percentile. We evaluate a deployed TPU using six production models from the MLP, CNN, and LSTM families that represented 95% of the provider's inference demand at the time. The comparison asks how specialization performs under these service constraints against the contemporary Haswell CPU and K80 GPU, with host interaction included.

The TPU is a host-controlled coprocessor connected over PCIe and designed for inference. Its dense systolic Matrix Multiply Unit contains 65,536 multiply-accumulate units operating on 8-bit integer operands, yielding a peak rate of 92 trillion operations per second. Software manages a 24 MiB Unified Buffer, supplemented by 4 MiB of accumulators, and execution follows a simple deterministic scheme. This combination supplies substantial arithmetic capacity, but neither peak rate nor a stationary workload characterization establishes sustained throughput. The dense hardware has no dedicated sparse-operation support, and Weight Memory bandwidth can constrain useful work. Roofline analysis [williams2009roofline] and counters expose memory limits in MLP/LSTM workloads, allowing low utilization to be interpreted alongside, rather than substituted for, delivered service throughput.

With latency limits enforced and host overhead included, TPU throughput is 14.5× Haswell by geometric mean and 29.2× by production-weighted mean; the corresponding K80 comparisons are 13.2× and 15.3×. These averages answer different aggregation questions, and the platforms use different numerical execution: quantized TPU inference is compared with floating-point CPU and GPU results. Total performance/Watt for complete servers is reported as 17–34× Haswell and 14–16× K80, depending on averaging. Higher incremental performance/Watt ratios subtract host-server power and therefore describe a different accounting boundary. Energy efficiency also depends on load: on CNN0, 10% offered load still consumes 88% of full-load TPU power. A separate model explores alternative hardware, including higher memory bandwidth; those results are predictions rather than deployed measurements. Together, the measurements and analysis expose both the benefit of inference specialization and its memory and power limitations. They do not establish purchase-price or total-ownership-cost advantages, because those quantities are undisclosed.

candidates.abstract: Datacenter inference hardware must deliver useful throughput within application response-time limits, making peak arithmetic rate an incomplete measure of value. We evaluate a deployed Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) using six production MLP, CNN, and LSTM models that represented 95% of the provider's inference demand at the time. The host-controlled coprocessor combines a dense systolic Matrix Multiply Unit with 65,536 multiply-accumulate units for 8-bit integer operands, a software-managed Unified Buffer, and deterministic execution. Its peak rate is 92 trillion operations per second. Measurements include host interaction overhead and enforce response-time limits. TPU throughput relative to contemporary Haswell is 14.5× by geometric mean and 29.2× by production-weighted mean; corresponding ratios to K80 are 13.2× and 15.3×. TPU inference is quantized while CPU and GPU results use floating point, so these ratios compare the evaluated platforms rather than equal datapaths. Complete-server total performance/Watt is 17–34× Haswell and 14–16× K80, depending on averaging; incremental ratios subtract host-server power. Roofline and counter analysis expose memory limits in MLP/LSTM workloads, showing why low utilization can coexist with high relative throughput. Light-load measurements also reveal weak energy proportionality. This evaluation establishes deployed inference behavior under service constraints; energy efficiency is a proxy, with purchase prices and total ownership cost undisclosed.
introduction: A datacenter inference accelerator is useful only to the extent that its throughput satisfies the service's response-time requirements. Increasing a batch can raise arithmetic throughput while making requests wait too long, so a comparison based solely on peak rate or unconstrained batching can miss the operating point that matters. The importance of the response-time tail is reflected in The Tail at Scale [dean2013tail]. Here, the concrete constraint for MLP0 is 7 ms at the 99th percentile. We evaluate a deployed TPU on six production models from the MLP, CNN, and LSTM families, representing 95% of the provider's inference demand at the time, against contemporary Intel Haswell and Nvidia K80 platforms. The measurements enforce application response-time limits and include host interaction overhead. This service-constrained evaluation asks what the deployed accelerator delivers across the observed workload mix, rather than inferring application performance from its arithmetic capacity.

The TPU is a host-controlled inference coprocessor connected over PCIe. Its dense systolic Matrix Multiply Unit contains 65,536 multiply-accumulate units operating on 8-bit integer operands, with a peak rate of 92 trillion operations per second. Software manages a 24 MiB Unified Buffer, complemented by 4 MiB of accumulators, and execution follows a simple deterministic scheme. The hardware has no dedicated sparse-operation support. Under the measured service constraints, Table6 reports throughput relative to Haswell of 14.5× by geometric mean and 29.2× by production-weighted mean; relative to K80, the corresponding ratios are 13.2× and 15.3×. Both summaries include host overhead, but their different weighting produces different conclusions about aggregate benefit. These are platform comparisons with differing numerical datapaths: TPU inference is quantized, whereas CPU and GPU results use floating point. For complete servers, total performance/Watt is 17–34× Haswell and 14–16× K80, depending on averaging. Incremental performance/Watt uses a different power boundary by subtracting host-server power and yields higher ratios.

The results also identify where the deployed design leaves performance and energy opportunities. Roofline analysis [williams2009roofline] and counters identify memory limits in the MLP/LSTM workloads, including the role of Weight Memory bandwidth; consequently, low utilization of the Matrix Multiply Unit can coexist with high throughput relative to the selected CPU and GPU baselines. Power does not fall proportionately with offered load: on CNN0 at 10% load, the TPU still consumes 88% of its full-load power. High complete-server performance/Watt therefore does not imply proportional energy savings across load levels. Energy efficiency is the disclosed proxy for value; negotiated purchase prices and total ownership cost are unavailable. A hardware model explores alternatives, including greater memory bandwidth, but those alternatives are distinct from the deployed measurements. Taken together, the measurements and analysis explain the evaluated TPU's strengths and limits for inference under response-time constraints, while preserving the contemporary baseline, workload, precision, and power-accounting scope of the comparison.
